Where it began

Graham Gooch was born at Whipps Cross in Leytonstone, east London, on 23 July 1953, and went to Norlington School and Leyton County High School. He first played for Essex in 1973, aged 19, and stayed with the county until 1997.

His Test career began quietly. On debut against Australia in 1975 he was out for nought in both innings, which at least got the hard part out of the way early. He was back in the side by 1978, and in 1980 Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year.

The player

Gooch played 118 Tests between 1975 and 1995, scoring 8,900 runs at 42.58 with 20 hundreds. He captained England in 34 of them. The West Indies, the most feared attack of the age, were on the receiving end of each of his first three Test hundreds, and against them in 1991 at Headingley he carried his bat for 154 not out in a match England won.

The summer of 1990 was his masterpiece. Against India at Lord's he made 333 and then 123, a total of 456 in one match. No one had ever made more runs in a single Test, and his 752 across that three-match series set another record.

What made him special

He stood tall and upright at the crease, with a high backlift and a heavy bat. As captain his fitness and hard work set the tone, and he averaged far more when leading the side (58.6) than when he was not.

He played in the World Cup finals of 1979, 1987 and 1992 finishing as runner-up each time, a record of reaching finals that very few can match. At the 1987 tournament he was the leading run-scorer, sweeping the Indian spinners to distraction during his 115 in the semi-final.

Away from the middle

Gooch was a key man in an Essex side that won the County Championship six times between 1979 and 1992. He holds the county record for runs in a season, 2559 in 1984, and made 94 first-class hundreds for them. In all top-level cricket he scored 67,057 runs, more than anyone.

Later he coached Essex and then England's batsmen, where Alastair Cook was among those who praised his influence. He was made an OBE, entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009, had two computer games named after him and supports West Ham United.

And finally

He bowled a little medium pace too, and in matches with nothing left to play for he liked to entertain by imitating the actions of other bowlers. In July 2000, at 46, he came back for one more first-class game and made 0 and 5. A man who began his Test career with a pair clearly knew how to keep a sense of proportion.
